title: Nothing at random
hookLine: let no act be done without a purpose (Meditations 4.2)

lines: WHY DID I COME IN HERE?
cards: A man walks into the kitchen and stops. Why did he come in here? He opens the fridge, looks, closes it.
He sets a pen down somewhere new and spends ten minutes hunting for it. Stretches of an ordinary day can run on their own, like a car driving itself while the driver thinks of something else.
Marcus Aurelius wrote an entry about exactly this, and it's barely a sentence long. Today: nothing at random.

teach.h: LET NO ACT BE DONE AT RANDOM.
teach.b: Let no act be done at random, Marcus writes in the second entry of book four, nor in any way other than by the principles of the craft. That's the whole entry.
The Stoics spoke of living well as an art, a skill like carpentry or medicine. A good carpenter doesn't swing the hammer at random; every cut is for the chair.
A life, Marcus says, can be built the same way, each act for something.

Back in book two he listed the ways a soul harms itself, and one was letting any act or movement happen without an aim. In his accounting, a day of random acts isn't neutral. It's a small harm, repeated.
Seneca made a similar point with a sailor's picture: if you don't know which harbor you're making for, no wind is the right wind.
Purpose doesn't have to be grand. I'm picking up my phone to answer my sister. I'm walking to the kitchen for water.
I'm going to this meeting to listen well. Small purposes, named, turn drift into steering. Marcus isn't asking for a rigid schedule or a life without rest.
Rest on purpose counts. A walk with no destination, chosen, counts. What he warns against is the act nobody chose, not even you.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 4.2 by naming the purpose of an ordinary act, such as picking up the phone, before doing it.

o: a Greek sailor who mapped the harbors of the Black Sea
the Roman Stoic who said no wind helps without a harbor in mind
a Roman poet who wrote songs about the winds and the sea

p: every cut is for the chair

s: Marcus's entry on random acts is very long
in book two Marcus says aimless acts harm the soul
he lists acting without an aim among the ways a soul harms itself.
Marcus says purpose means never resting
the warning is against acts nobody chose; chosen rest counts.

games.q: you have twenty free minutes. you could scroll, or do something else. what fits Meditations 4.2?
o: scroll: it's free time, after all.
choose something, even rest, and name why.
fill it with any task to stay busy.
games.why: Marcus asks only that no act be done at random. rest, chosen on purpose, passes his test.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing you'll do in the next hour, making tea, opening your email, walking to the car, and name its purpose in a few words. Picture doing it with that purpose in mind, start to finish, nothing extra.
Notice how the same act feels when it's chosen.

wordCard.voice: Seneca, who said that without a harbor in mind, no wind is the right wind, the way Marcus warned against acts done at random. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'at random, without aim': the word Marcus uses for the act he warns against in 4.2.

carryVoice: Your line: on purpose. Rest counts too, when it's chosen on purpose. See you tomorrow.
